MorphoHand · SR2 hand, real_v1 screwdriver · contact models and the printed fingertip · 6 October 2026 · built 2026-10-06 11:33

Friction creep, the printed TPU fingertip and the deployed three-finger reorientation in MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Drake

MuJoCo’s friction creep falls as 1/impratio: at impratio 10 000 the 1 mm sphere pads creep 0.31 µm/s and turn 0.013 °/s under half their slip load, against 31 µm/s and 1.2 °/s at the bed’s impratio 100 and 0.20 µm/s and 0.0084 °/s in Drake at 1 ms, while slip onset, twist onset and the brake move by at most 3 % and 1°; noslip removes only the translational part and does not run in MuJoCo-Warp. The printed SR2 fingertip is a TPU block 14.8 mm wide with 2.7–6 mm fillets; every earlier contact study used a 10.55 mm sphere. Packed with 1 mm spheres, the block matches Drake’s hydroelastic torsion onset within 5 %, and its fillet sets the pinch’s friction arm at 1.2–3.0 times the sphere’s. On the eight deployed hands’ three-finger turn, the pads and Drake give the same outcome on 94 % of paired seeds with the 6 mm block and 92 % with the 2.7 mm block, against 42 % for MuJoCo’s single-mesh point contact and 67 % for the legacy box; the sphere tip holds the tool on 7 and 12 of 72 seeds in MuJoCo and Drake where the 6 mm block holds 59 and 61. No contact model reproduces the bench hand by hand: D2, held 10/10 on the bench, drops in every condition at the calibrated servo gain, and with the tool resting on its post (every bench scene since 2026-08-29 starts it 12.5 mm inside the post) only the shipped servo gain kp 30 turns it by tens of degrees, 29–63° on 7 hands against the bench’s 33–70°, while holding 72 of 72 seeds. The co-design section proposes scoring candidate fingertips on task success and on this agreement between simulators together.

Terms and metrics

creep
Steady sliding of a pinched tool while its load stays below the slip load. Translational creep: axial sliding speed during a 1 s hold at half the axial force at which the tool slips (bed task 1), in µm/s. Twist creep: turning speed about the pinch axis during a 1 s hold at half the torque at which it spins (bed task 2), in °/s. Rigid Coulomb friction gives zero.
pad force N
Normal force of one fingertip on the tool on the two-pad rig, in N; the rig holds it constant with a force-controlled rail.
slip onset μeff
Axial force at which the tool starts to slide, divided by 2N; rigid Coulomb friction with μ = 1 gives 1.000.
friction arm r̄
Torque about the pinch axis at which the tool starts to spin, divided by 2μN, in mm per pad (bed task 2). A pad transmits at most μN r̄ about its normal. Static arm: the force-weighted mean distance of the contact points (or hydroelastic faces) from their centre, in mm, with the tool pressed at N and no load.
brake end, N at 45°
Bed task 5: the tool, its centre of mass 15 mm from the pinch axis, hangs in the pinch while the pad force falls from 6 to 0.2 N over 4 s. Brake end is the final swing angle (90° = hanging), N at 45° the pad force when the swing passes 45°.
impratio, noslip, tr
MuJoCo solver settings. impratio scales the friction rows’ stiffness relative to the normal row (elliptic cone). noslip_iterations runs a second solve of the friction rows without softness after the main solve. tr is the sphere pads’ relaxation time: their contact damping divided by their stiffness.
sphere pad
A fingertip surface packed with 0.75 mm collision spheres 1 mm apart, each a spring of stiffness E/h · As (As its share of the surface, h the foundation depth). Contact patch, centre of pressure and torsion follow from which spheres touch.
contact representation
Sphere: the 10.55 mm sphere at the end of real_hand.xml, one MuJoCo contact. Legacy box: the sharp box (21.1 × 14.8 mm face) the plans were exported against, one MuJoCo contact. TPU mesh: the printed block as one convex mesh, one MuJoCo contact. TPU pads: the block covered with 1 mm sphere pads. Drake: the same shape as a compliant hydroelastic body (E 10 MPa, relaxation 0.01 s) against the rigid tool.
fillet rf
Radius of the rounded edges of the printed fingertip block, in mm. rf = 0 is the sharp box; the palmar face is flat over (14.8 − 2rf) × (22 − 2rf) mm.
held
A reorientation seed holds the tool when, at the end of the bench schedule’s 1.5 s hold, at least two fingers touch it and its centre is within 20 mm of its height at the end of the grip. Reported as held seeds over seeds.
turn
Net change of the tool’s tilt from the end of the grip to the end of the hold, in degrees, positive toward vertical (the plan’s direction). Bench values are the net turn on held trials (paper/figures/ranking.json).
seed
One placement of the tool on the post: seed 0 at the plan’s pose, seeds 1–8 (and 9–63 on the GPU) shifted by normal draws of sd 2 mm in x and y and 2° in yaw. The same seed is the same placement in every simulator.
paired agreement
For two conditions run on the same hands and seeds, the fraction of (hand, seed) pairs with the same held outcome, and the median absolute difference in turn on pairs held in both.
cost
µs per step: median wall time of one 1 ms physics step on one CPU core. µs per world-step: GPU wall time of one step divided by the number of parallel worlds.

Creep in MuJoCo's soft friction

MuJoCo’s friction rows are soft: under a steady sub-threshold load each loaded contact behaves as a damper, so the tool slides at a constant speed instead of sticking. At steady creep the friction row carries Rtft = −b v with b = 2/(d0tc) and Rt = (1 − d0)Λ/(d0 impratio). With the pad stiffness calibrated at load, K = 1/(tc2(1 − d0)Λ) and tr = 2tc, the creep speed of n loaded spheres sharing a tangential load Ft is

v ≈ Ft / (impratio · n · K · tr),

linear in the load per sphere, inverse in impratio and in the relaxation time, and independent of the step. The 1 mm pads creep 31 µm/s at 1 N and turn 1.2 °/s under half their twist load; Drake creeps 0.20 µm/s and turns 0.0084 °/s at a 1 ms step, about 155 and 145 times less. Drake also creeps: its regularised friction gives a speed that grows with the step, 0.91 µm/s at 5 ms. Table 1 crosses impratio 100–10 000, noslip 1–10 iterations and tr 0.02–0.1 s on the bed’s pull, twist, shake and brake tasks (406 rows, docs/experiments/20261005-contact_bed/creep.jsonl).

impratio lowers both creeps as 1/impratio. At 10 000 the pads creep 0.31 µm/s and turn 0.013 °/s, inside Drake’s own range between its 1 and 5 ms steps; slip onset stays at μeff 1.005, the twist onset arm moves from 0.924 to 0.956 mm (Drake 0.987), and the brake ends at 87.3° against Drake’s 87.3°. The rig’s step cost does not change. On the full hand chain of 2026-10-02 (pick, lift, braked swing, peg-hole insert) the physics time per simulated second is 73, 103, 124 and 148 ms at impratio 100, 1000, 3000 and 10 000; the chain completes in all four, the swing ends at 90.5, 91.4, 91.5 and 91.6° (Drake hydroelastic 91.3°) and the lifted tool’s lean drops from 2.4 to 0.6°. MuJoCo-Warp 3.6 accepts any impratio.

noslip removes the translational creep and reverses its sign: −1.6 µm/s at 10 iterations, a drift against the load of about 5 % of the original speed. It barely touches the pad’s twist creep, 0.96 °/s at 10 iterations; its projected Gauss–Seidel pass converges slowly on the torsion mode shared by ~15 spheres (30 iterations 0.73 °/s at 48 µs, 100 iterations 0.24 °/s at 116 µs, 300 iterations 0.15 °/s at 145 µs). MuJoCo-Warp 3.6 raises NotImplementedError for any noslip_iterations > 0 (external/mujoco_warp/mujoco_warp/_src/io.py), so it cannot reach the RL pipeline.

A longer relaxation time lowers creep as 1/tr but makes the pinch torque depend on spin rate, as Drake’s relaxation time does: with tr 0.05 s the brake swings through to 91.7° at 1 ms and stops at 76.5° at 5 ms, and passes 80° at 1.13 N instead of 0.40 N; with 0.1 s the tool leaves the pinch at the 5 ms step.

Heavier objects. Mass enters the creep only through the load. With the stiffness calibrated per object at load (the 10-05 pad calibration), a heavier tool held at the same pad force creeps faster in proportion to the extra tangential load until it slips. Held at the same fraction of its slip load, it creeps as roughly the square root of the load, because more spheres engage: from 0.5 to 3 N the pads go from 23 to 53 µm/s, 2.35 times for 6 times the load. At the bed’s impratio a 10 s hold at half the slip load moves the tool 0.31 mm and turns it 12.1°; at impratio 1000 these become 0.031 mm and 1.2°.

On the deployed three-finger turn (Table 7) impratio 100 agrees with Drake best; each step toward Drake’s creep loses held seeds on two of eight hands. Keep impratio 100 for manipulation and raise it only for long static holds, where 10 000 reproduces Drake’s creep at +103 % physics time on the hand.

The printed TPU fingertip

Every contact study from 2026-10-01 to 10-05 modelled the SR2 fingertip as the 10.55 mm sphere at the end of assets/mjcf/real_v1/real_hand.xml, and the deployed plans were exported against a sharp box 21.1 mm wide and 14.8 mm long (scene_mutate.set_finger_flat_pads). The printed tip is neither. The CAD of 2026-08-27 (~/Downloads/fingertip (3).stl, the TPU insert on fingertip_mount (2).stl) is a block 17.0 mm deep, 14.8 mm wide along the PIP axis and 21.4–22.0 mm long; its palmar face sits 10.55 mm from the finger axis, flush with the link capsule, its end 37.16 mm from the PIP axis, and its front and end edges are rounded with rf = 2.7–3.0 mm while the back, on the mount’s 3 mm plate, is square. On 2026-10-04 the fillet of the printed tips was given as 6 mm, so both radii are modelled. scripts/fingertip_geometry.py builds the block for MuJoCo (a convex mesh, or 1 mm sphere pads on every face but the back and the mount side, 796 spheres per tip at rf 6, foundation depth 8.5 mm) and Drake (a compliant convex, E 10 MPa), and scripts/tpu_tip_rig.py puts it on the bed’s two-pad rig with the PIP axis along the tool’s axis, as in the bench grasp.

The fillet sets the pinch’s friction arm. In Drake at 0.5 N the contact strip is 4.4 mm long for rf 6, 10.0 for 2.7 and 14.8 for the sharp box, against a 3.3 mm disc for the sphere; the static arm is 1.12, 2.45 and 3.70 mm against the sphere’s 0.82. The sphere pads reproduce the twist onset of the filleted blocks: 1.273 against 1.257 mm at 1 N and 1.459 against 1.519 at 3 N for rf 6, 2.525 against 2.496 and 2.736 against 2.618 for 2.7 (Table 3, Figure 3). On the sharp box the pads put extra spheres along both side edges and overstate the arm by about 8 %. A single convex mesh gives MuJoCo one contact point and no torsion; with multiccd it gives five points along the line, and its arm falls with force and changes with step (0.96 mm at 1 ms, 0.68 mm at 5 ms, 3 N), so it is not a usable torsion model.

The brake (Table 3) separates the tips. With the sphere the tool swings to 87–88°. With the 6 mm block it reaches 45° at the same force within 3 % (MuJoCo 0.946 N, Drake 0.968 N) and stalls at 77.3° in MuJoCo and 83.1° in Drake at 0.2 N: as the tool swings, its contact line turns from across the 2.8 mm flat to along the 10 mm flat, the arm grows and the remaining gravity torque cannot overcome it. The 2.7 mm block swings at a third of the force (0.34–0.50 N at 45°) and slides 2–8 mm along its axis, more at 5 ms in both simulators. impratio 10 000 does not change the brake on either block.

The deployed three-finger turn in each contact model

The deployed reorientation is the open-loop three-finger turn of the SR2 paper: the hand closes on the screwdriver lying on a post with its palm fixed, and a joint-space trajectory moves all three fingertips so that the tool turns toward vertical about the pinch axis. The bench ran it 77 times on the eight deployed hands (paper/figures/ranking.json). Here each hand’s plan replays unchanged (2536 rollouts in MuJoCo, MuJoCo-Warp and Drake): 0.8 s grip, the plan’s 4 s trajectory (1.3 s more grip, a 1.1 s turn, hold), 1.5 s hold, then 4 s more; the finger servos are the calibrated position servos (kp 0.5, kv 0.02, 0.35 N m, joint damping 0.5, measured masses), friction is the scenes’ 2.4, the step 1 ms, and nine tool placements per hand are the same seeds in every simulator (scripts/reorient_backends.py; MuJoCo-Warp runs 64 seeds in one batch). The harness reproduces the 2026-09-16 replay where that replay’s outcome is stable (D7 21.9 ± 4.1° against 21.6 ± 3.8°, D2, D4, D5 within 3°).

Every bench scene starts the tool inside its post. scene_mutate.set_object_platform puts the tool’s centre and the post’s top at the same height, so the 12.5 mm tool begins 12.5 mm deep in the post (contact distance −12.5 mm in the compiled scene) and is thrown out in the first 20 ms. Every replay of a bench plan since 2026-08-29 carries this start, including the plant-correction gate, Table IV’s simulated column and the 2026-09-16 turn studies; the 17° of tilt those replays found “already in the grip” is mostly the ejection. Here the post is shortened so the tool rests on it at the plan’s pose (2536 rows in reorient_*.jsonl; the rows with the original post are kept in superseded_tool_in_post/). With the tool resting, D7’s plan holds the tool on every seed in MuJoCo and Drake with the legacy box and turns it 1–9°, where the bench turned it 33°.

Three things move the outcome more than the choice of simulator. The fingertip: the sphere drops the tool on most hands in both simulators, the TPU block holds it on most. The servo: with the shipped gain (kp 30) the legacy box holds 72 of 72 seeds and turns the tool 29–63° on all but one hand, the bench’s range (the TPU pads: 72 of 72), where the calibrated kp 0.5 holds 25 of 72 and turns at most 11°. The 2026-09-02 calibration that chose kp 0.5, and its check against the bench (retention 0.94 against 0.92, cosine 0.638 against 0.593 on D7), ran on scenes that start the tool inside its post, so both have to be repeated. Friction: μ 1 instead of 2.4 takes the legacy box from 25 to 15 held seeds of 72. No condition reproduces the bench hand by hand; the TPU models rank the hands against the bench (ρ down to −0.8), because D2, which the bench holds 10/10, drops in every condition at kp 0.5 while D5 and D6, held 2–3 of 10 on the bench, hold in most conditions.

Table 6. Paired agreement on identical hands and tool placements.

Matching Drake’s creep does not bring the turn closer to Drake. With the 6 mm pads at impratio 10 000, D3 holds 3/9 and D4 5/9 seeds against 6/9 and 8/9 at 100 and 9/9 and 8/9 in Drake; on the GPU the same change takes D3 from 49/64 to 30/64 and D4 from 54/64 to 36/64. The lost seeds hold through the grip exactly as at impratio 100 and drop 0.4–0.8 s into the turn, the tool landing on its end. The solver converges in both (median 1–4 Newton iterations, at most 17 of the 100 allowed, on D3 seed 0), so the difference is the friction law: soft friction lets the pads slide while the fingers move, and at impratio 10 000 they hold until the cone limit and then let go.

Fingertip co-design for task and simulability

The fingertip sets what the task does: the friction arm of a pinch differs by 1.4–4.6 times between the sphere, the two fillets and the sharp box at 0.5 N, and the deployed turn holds the tool on 7–12 of 72 seeds with the sphere and 59–61 with the 6 mm block. Whether two simulators agree about the task depends on how that fingertip’s contact is represented (Table 6). Finger-shape optimisation has a long record for the first; choosing a fingertip by how consistently different contact models simulate its task has none that we found.

Prior work

  • Fingertip and finger form for a task. Fit2Form (Ha, Agrawal and Song, CoRL 2020) generates parallel-jaw finger pairs per object with a learned fitness; DGDM (Xu, Ha, Song, CoRL 2024) generates manipulator shapes from task interaction profiles with a dynamics-guided diffusion model; Meixner, Hazard and Pollard (Humanoids 2019) co-optimise hand morphology and control under explicit placement and model uncertainty and report designs that use every surface of the hand; Ye et al. (arXiv 2511.13710, 2025) add a planar fingertip modification to a dexterous hand and optimise it with control through a differentiable neural-physics surrogate, 82.5 % zero-shot precision grasping; the contact-primitive fingertips of US 11 185 986 match printed soft tips to clusters of local grasp geometry.
  • Curvature for in-hand rolling. Chen, Lu, Colgate and Lynch (arXiv 2607.12105, 2026) compare flat, spherical and two cylindrical tips of the same envelope on an Allegro hand rolling objects: the cylinder curved along the rolling direction gives 2.29 turns and 86 % success, the sphere 1.39 and 86 %, the flat 1.46 and 69 %, the cylinder across it 0.78 and 67 %. A filleted block is a cylinder in one direction and a flat in the other, so the same orientation question applies to the SR2 tip.
  • Soft-finger contact. Xydas and Kao (IJRR 1999) give the contact radius a ∝ Nγ with 0 ≤ γ ≤ 1/3 and an elliptical limit surface in force and torsion; the elastic-foundation law used here is γ = 1/4. Spiers, Calli and Dollar (RA-L 2018) switch a finger between gripping and sliding with a surface that recesses above 1.2–2.5 N, a mechanical answer to the hold-versus-slide trade the brake exposes. Babin and Gosselin (IJRR 2018) design fingers and a fingernail-like edge for picking thin objects off flat surfaces, the case a round or blunt tip handles worst.
  • Simulators as an uncertainty set. Elandt et al. (IROS 2019) give the pressure-field model, Masterjohn et al. (RA-L 2022) its velocity-level patch approximation and Castro et al. (T-RO 2023) Drake’s SAP solver; Horak and Trinkle (RA-L 2019) and Le Lidec et al. (arXiv 2304.06372) compare contact models on grasping and wedging scenes and find qualitatively different outcomes once several contacts act; PolySim (arXiv 2510.01708, 2025) trains humanoid policies across several physics engines to cover their differences; Kriegman et al. (RoboSoft 2020) show that the sim-to-real gap of soft robots depends on morphology and select designs that transfer. None of these uses agreement between contact models as a criterion for the hardware itself.

Formulation

Let a fingertip be a parameter vector g: fillet radius across the face and along it, face width, a face curvature (flat to a cylinder of radius R), an optional rigid nail edge at the end face (protrusion and thickness), and the TPU stiffness E. For a task suite T and an ensemble of contact models M (MuJoCo point, MuJoCo sphere pads, Drake hydroelastic, Newton hydroelastic), each run on the same seeds, score

J(g) = meanm∈M successm(g) − λ · disagreementM(g) − η · cost(g),

with disagreement the fraction of paired seeds on which the models’ outcomes differ (Table 6’s first column, complemented) and cost the GPU time per world-step of the pad model. The 2026-09 bench plans held the tool on seven of eight hands in the simulator they were planned in and on 2–10 of 10 trials on the bench; in Table 4 the held count of that planning model (legacy box, MuJoCo point contact) differs from Drake’s for the same plan by four or more seeds of nine on 2 hands. The quick-release tips of the SR2 hand (paper Sec. II-B) make each candidate a print and a swap, so the ensemble can be checked against hardware at every round.

Tasks

  • the deployed three-finger turn on D1–D8 (this page; held fraction and turn);
  • the pinch brake and swing (bed task 5) and the paper’s pusher and wield (2026-10-02), where torsion must be low to swing and high to hold;
  • a thin-object pick: a 20 mm coin, a 1 mm card and an M3 washer flat on the table, lifted by a two-finger pinch that has to get an edge under the object, the task a sphere tip fails by construction;
  • a held tool under a 2 g shake (bed task 4), the retention case where creep and torsion both act.

Search

Each candidate is a mesh from fingertip_geometry.py generalised to these parameters; its static signature on the rig (patch area, torsion arm against force and against contact-line angle) takes seconds in MuJoCo and Drake and screens out shapes whose two models disagree statically. The survivors run the task suite on MuJoCo-Warp (64–512 seeds per design, 20 µs per world-step with the pads) with Drake on nine paired seeds for the disagreement term; a cross-entropy or Bayesian search over five or six parameters needs on the order of 100 designs. Three designs from the front go to the printer and the bench.

Next measurements

  1. Confirm the printed fillet. Measure one printed tip with a radius gauge (6 mm per 2026-10-04, 2.7–3.0 mm in the 08-27 CAD). The two radii give the brake a 3× different swing force on this page; if a third radius is printed, add it with --tips tpu<r>.
  2. Fix the post in the scene generator. scene_mutate.set_object_platform should place the tool’s centre one radius above the post. Re-run the plant-correction gate (scripts/plant_drop_gate.py) and the eight-hand bench replay (scripts/real_v1_bench_plants.py) on corrected scenes; if the gate’s retention match (0.94 against 0.92) does not survive, the plant calibration of 2026-09-02 rests on the ejection.
  3. Bench measurement of the tip’s torsion. Pinch the screwdriver between two printed tips on the bench at 0.5, 1 and 3 N and raise a torque about the pinch axis with a hanging mass on a 50 mm arm until it turns; the sphere model predicts r̄ 0.84–1.31 mm, the 6 mm block 1.13–1.52, the 2.7 mm block about 2.5. This measurement decides which model the brake and the turn should be planned in.
  4. Newton on the hand. Port the bench scene to Newton hydroelastic with the TPU mesh (scripts/contact_bed_newton.py has the rig); the bed found Newton’s torsion 2.3–2.9 times the hydroelastic law, so check the rig’s TPU twist first.
  5. First co-design round. Sweep rf ∈ {0, 1.5, 2.7, 4, 6, 7.4} on the bench turn in MuJoCo pads and Drake (nine seeds each, about 2 h on four cores) and plot held fraction and paired agreement against rf; build the thin-object pick scene and run the sphere, the 6 mm block and a block with a 1 mm nail.
